Sementara itu, Mahkamah Tinggi pada Julai 2023 memerintahkan TH Heavy Engineering (THHE) membayar ganti rugi RM288.7 juta kepada Globalmariner Offshore Services (GMOS) kerana melanggar perjanjian pemegang saham mereka.
Pegangan saham TH dalam THHE dipindahkan kepada Urusharta Jamaah pada 2018.

Syaza Shukri dari Universiti Islam Antarabangsa Malaysia turut menyokong penelitian lebih menyeluruh bagi menentukan sama ada usaha sama itu menunjukkan masalah tadbir urus lebih besar, selain mengenal pasti langkah bagi mengelakkan perkara sama berulang.
"Saya berpendapat syarikat terjejas perlu tampil mengemukakan aduan kerana mereka perlu mempunyai keyakinan bahawa setiap aduan akan diberikan pertimbangan adil."

Jelasnya, pakar luar bebas boleh dipertanggungjawabkan untuk menilai aduan itu, manakala Jabatan Audit Negara dan Jawatankuasa Kira-kira Wang Negara (PAC) juga boleh dijadikan saluran bagi penelitian lanjut.

Katanya, akauntabiliti perlu disusuli penyelesaian praktikal sambil memberi amaran kegagalan mengambil tindakan susulan secara berkesan boleh menjejaskan keyakinan orang ramai terhadap sistem sedia ada.
Zaharuddin mencadangkan audit bebas terhadap penghakiman belum selesai dan tuntutan komersial disahkan, di samping mewujudkan proses telus untuk mengenal pasti aset boleh diperoleh semula.
Beliau turut menyarankan satu mekanisme dengan had masa diwujudkan bagi menyelesaikan tuntutan sah melalui tindakan penguatkuasaan, penstrukturan semula atau penyelesaian secara rundingan.
"Pampasan perlu berasaskan liabiliti undang-undang yang telah dibuktikan, bukannya tekanan politik.

"Kejayaan dalam memastikan akauntabiliti tidak patut diukur berdasarkan jumlah bekas eksekutif disiasat, sebaliknya sejauh mana kebenaran dapat didedahkan, jumlah wang diperoleh semula secara sah serta bilangan tuntutan sah diselesaikan."
e34a5732cf313f5e: PETALING JAYA: The government has been urged to set up an independent panel to investigate complaints from businesses affected by troubled Tabung Haji-linked ventures, and explore avenues for redress.
Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri of Global Asia Consulting said scrutiny should extend beyond the pilgrim fund’s losses to how its partners, suppliers and creditors have been treated.

“My proposal is straightforward: establish a confidential, time-limited evidence submission process, protect credible complainants against retaliation, and publish the panel’s findings without compromising ongoing legal proceedings,” he told FMT.
He proposed a panel, preferably under parliamentary oversight, comprising specialists in forensic accounting, corporate law, insolvency and public-sector governance.
“If public institutions are expected to protect people’s savings, they must also be held accountable for how they exercise power over other people’s businesses.”
Zaharuddin said the review must distinguish ordinary commercial losses from contractual disputes, governance failures and possible criminal wrongdoing.
“Not every failed investment is corruption, but neither should every questionable transaction be conveniently dismissed as a business decision,” he said.

The call comes after former TH chief executive officer Johan Abdullah and former chief financial officer Rozaida Omar were charged on Oct 22 for allegedly using inflated property valuations to facilitate RM3.3 billion in hibah payments in 2017.
Both pleaded not guilty.
Separately, FGV reported in November 2019 that its accumulated share of losses from Trurich, its 50:50 plantation venture with TH, stood at approximately RM234 million.
Meanwhile, in July 2023, the High Court awarded Globalmariner Offshore Services (GMOS) RM288.7 million in damages against TH Heavy Engineering (THHE) for breaching their shareholders’ agreement.
TH’s stake in THHE was transferred to Urusharta Jamaah in 2018.

Syaza Shukri of International Islamic University Malaysia expressed support for wider scrutiny to establish whether the ventures pointed to broader governance problems and to identify measures that could prevent their recurrence.
“I think, yes, businesses should come forward because they should have confidence that their complaints would receive a fair hearing,” she said.
She said independent external experts could be tasked with assessing complaints, while the auditor-general and the Public Accounts Committee could also serve as avenues for further scrutiny.
Syaza said accountability must deliver practical remedies, warning that ineffective follow-through could undermine confidence in the system.
Zaharuddin proposed an independent audit of outstanding judgments and verified commercial claims, alongside a transparent process to identify recoverable assets.
He also called for a time-bound mechanism to resolve valid claims through enforcement, restructuring or negotiated settlements.
“Compensation must follow established legal liability, not political pressure,” he said.

“Ultimately, the success of accountability should not be measured by how many former executives are investigated, but by how much truth is uncovered, how much money is lawfully recovered, and how many legitimate claims are finally resolved.”
f572520be77c794a: KLUANG: For one father, the hardest part of prison was not simply being confined - it was being away from his family, especially his five children, while the days towards Deepavali seemed to move slowly.

The 47-year-old, who wishes to be known as Azroy, had been serving a six-month sentence for drug-related offences. At times, he said, the separation became so overwhelming, he would cry alone while counting down the days until he could return home.

That return came sooner than expected: he was among 96 individuals freed from Kluang Prison by the prisons department's licence-based release programme - a community-based rehabilitation initiative - after passing the required assessments and screening.
His release came two months ahead of schedule - just days before Deepavali.
“I am so grateful to have been released in time for Deepavali this year,” he told Bernama. “I cannot wait to celebrate with my family, especially my five children, and become a better person.”
For Suba, 42, the news was equally unexpected. She had spent nine months behind bars after being detained for stealing money from a shop, and had expected to remain there until the end of December.
Instead, she learnt she would be going home in time for a celebration she had never before spent away from her family.
“I am so happy that I can celebrate Deepavali with my children, as I have never celebrated it without them. Otherwise, I would have had to spend it in prison," she said.
Suba said she regretted the actions that led to her imprisonment, while Azroy described his time served as a lesson he does not want to repeat.

Johor prisons deputy director Walace Nawon said the 96 people released from Kluang Prison comprised 92 men and four women, all of whom had displayed good behaviour and passed several screening processes.
For individuals like Azroy and Suba, being released does not erase what came before; yet, it offers both a chance to begin again.
Both are back with their families, carrying the hope that the festival’s promise of light after darkness can mark the start of something better.

4bf2facb64e26158: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian women have made progress in workforce participation and career advancement over the years, but experts believe a gap remains between the opportunities available to them and their ability to fully benefit from them.

They think women's empowerment should not be measured solely by their labour force participation rate but also by the quality of jobs they hold, their access to leadership positions and their ability to control their income and make independent financial decisions.

The Department of Statistics Malaysia (DOSM) recorded a female labour force participation rate of 56.6 per cent, compared with 83.3 percent for men, in the fourth quarter of 2025, indicating considerable room for improvement in women's economic participation.
SHARING OF RESPONSIBILITIES

Universiti Utara Malaysia (UUM) Centre for Applied Psychology, Policy and Social Work senior lecturer Associate Prof Dr Rajwani Md Zain said the true measure of empowerment is the extent to which women have the choice to work, advance their careers and build financial security.

She said one of the main challenges facing women in the country is the unequal sharing of family caregiving responsibilities, particularly for single mothers and female heads of households. This is compounded by the high cost of childcare, especially in urban areas, and a lack of childcare services that align with the working hours of mothers.

Workplace cultures that lack an understanding of family needs also present a challenge – for instance, mothers who require time to breastfeed their children may not be granted any flexibility by their employers.

"These challenges vary according to income, location, employment status and the level of family support available. Therefore, (women) empowerment policies must pay particular attention to single mothers, low-income women, those in rural areas and women working in the informal sector," she said in an interview with Bernama recently.

Elaborating, Rajwani said childcare and family responsibilities significantly influence women's decisions to return to work. For instance, after childbirth, mothers have to adjust to physical recovery, breastfeeding, newborn care routines and emotional changes, while also having to meet the demands of their jobs.
Without adequate family support and access to affordable childcare, returning to work can become a daunting challenge for many mothers.
LONG-TERM CONSEQUENCES
Citing DOSM's 2025 time-use data, Rajwani said women spent about six hours and seven minutes daily on unpaid domestic and caregiving responsibilities, including looking after babies.
This, she said, could lead women to reduce their working hours, turn down promotion opportunities or even leave their jobs altogether.
"For example, when a promotion involves relocating to another area, many women are reluctant to move away from their families.
"The consequences can be far-reaching as the loss of income also affects work experience, salary progression and retirement savings in the future.
"Women's decisions to leave their jobs should not be viewed merely as a personal choice, but examined in the context of the constraints they face and the support available to them," she said.
She said reports of child neglect and abuse at childcare institutions have heightened parents' concerns about their children's safety.

Commenting on the increase in maternity leave entitlement from 360 to 490 days for civil servants, as announced by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim during the 2027 Budget presentation, Rajwani described the move as recognition of mothers' recovery needs and family responsibilities.
She said the extended leave could help mothers navigate the crucial early period after childbirth more comfortably and reduce pressure to return to work earlier.
Postnatal care support could also help mothers manage their own recovery and their babies' needs, making the transition back to work easier.

"However, this measure must be complemented by support after maternity leave ends. This includes affordable, quality childcare centres with operating hours suited to working parents, particularly shift workers; breastfeeding facilities; and flexible working arrangements where job requirements permit.
"Employers should consider providing such facilities or, at the very least, offering greater flexibility to mothers, especially first-time mothers," she added.
WOMEN EMPOWERING WOMEN

Meanwhile, pointing to the care economy, which has the potential to create employment and entrepreneurship opportunities in the care services sector, Rajwani said it would enable more women to enter or return to the workforce.
She said caregiving services should not be limited to infant care but should also cover maternal care during the confinement period.

"Opportunities in prenatal and postnatal care include providing daily assistance at home, preparing meals, helping with household management and caring for mothers and babies, according to the training and competencies of service providers.
"This could also include clinical services, provided by qualified professionals," she said.

On Sept 15, Women, Family and Community Development Minister Datuk Seri Nancy Shukri was reported as saying that 42.8 percent of the 4.89 million women outside the labour force cited household responsibilities and caring for family members as their main reasons for not participating in the workforce.

Commenting on the figures, Rajwani said they highlighted the link between access to caregiving support and women's economic participation, rather than indicating the number of new jobs that could be created.
She said any vacancy arising from women's withdrawal from the labour force could be filled by workers of either gender.

"Developing the care economy requires collaboration among the government, private sector and communities to provide more secure career opportunities, social protection and quality services that families can afford.

"The sector's success should not be measured solely by the well-being of those receiving care but also by whether the people providing these services receive proper recognition, protection and fair remuneration," she said.
PLATFORM SUPPORT
Among the organisations tapping into the potential of the care services sector is iBidan, a home-based prenatal and postnatal care platform.
iBidan founder Shannon Eu said her platform leverages women's traditional caregiving skills to help them earn an income without having to establish or operate their own care service centres.
It also provides mothers with opportunities to balance their career aspirations with family responsibilities.

iBidan connects experienced midwives with clients through a structured booking system, operational support, professional skills development and opportunities for midwives to build more organised careers.
The platform now has a network of more than 500 midwives in Malaysia and Singapore.
"This approach demonstrates how existing caregiving skills can be integrated into a modern service delivery system to create professional career opportunities in maternal care," Eu said.

She also said that iBidan recently signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Wanita Berdaya Selangor (WBS) in conjunction with the Selangor International Care Expo (SICE) 2026 that was held here recently.

WBS, a subsidiary of Menteri Besar Selangor (Incorporated), supports the Selangor government's women's empowerment agenda. The signing ceremony was also attended by WBS chief executive officer Siti Faridah Abdul Samad and Selangor state executive council member Anfaal Saari.

"This collaboration provides both organisations with an opportunity to explore initiatives in community education and postnatal maternal care support, as well as develop the professional skills and careers of midwives, whose jobs hold both economic and social value.

"Through this MoU, iBidan and WBS hope to explore collaborative opportunities that will support the development of a skilled female workforce and contribute to a more inclusive and sustainable care economy," Eu said.

In conjunction with SICE 2026, iBidan also organised a special forum, titled 'Building Careers. Changing Lives – Real Stories from the Women Behind iBidan', featuring three midwives who shared their experiences, challenges and career opportunities in the caregiving services sector.

The forum also explored how professional skills, easy access to clients and platform support could help women rebuild their careers while improving their families' well-being. For more information on iBidan, please visit www.ibidan.com.my or www.ibidan.com.sg. — BERNAMA

Ikan masin meets Italian pasta, anyone?

The couple subsequently expanded their ambitions. In 2018, when an adjoining end-lot unit became available, they seized the opportunity to launch La Carne, a separate concept offering English Sunday roast, Peruvian-style chicken, wood-fired pizzas and pastas infused with Malaysian ingredients.
The two businesses, however, eventually presented a different set of challenges.
“After about two years of operating both businesses, the economic climate became increasingly challenging, and we had to make some difficult decisions,” Meor recalls.
“Sales were becoming increasingly inconsistent and declining, and we had three kids to think about too. We had to be realistic about the financial pressure of keeping two outlets running.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Calzone and pizzas. — Picture courtesy of Kopimeo x La Carne
Rather than persist with two separate operations, the couple decided to relinquish one shop lot and consolidate both concepts under one roof.

The result was Kopimeo x La Carne, combining the neighbourhood café atmosphere of Kopimeo with La Carne’s more adventurous approach to food. The move also reduced overheads and simplified team management, allowing them to concentrate their staff and resources in one space.
For Meor, the experience reinforced an important lesson about entrepreneurship: enthusiasm for food is not enough to sustain a business.
“Loving food and running an F&B business are two very different things. Passion alone isn’t enough; you also have to understand cash flow, manage people and control costs,” he says.
It is a lesson that has informed their approach to the menu, too, particularly Iena’s experiments with combining Western cooking techniques and local flavours.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Spicy Beef Stroganoff (left). Salmon Belly Thai Red Curry (right). — Pictures courtesy of Kopimeo x La Carne
Her culinary curiosity was shaped in part by her father, who experimented with ingredients while living abroad, finding substitutes that brought familiar Malaysian flavours into unfamiliar dishes.

“When he was living abroad, he experimented with whatever ingredients he had available,” she says. “He might add ikan masin to a pasta dish in place of anchovies, or dried chillies to a beef stew for a more familiar Malaysian kick.”

That playful spirit eventually found its way into Kopimeo x La Carne’s signature dishes. From their Russian inspired Spicy Beef Stroganoff to the cold-smoked Gulai Lemak Daging Berasap, there’s always a bit of East meets West going on.

Even an ingredient as ubiquitous as salmon can be reinvented: the Salmon Belly Thai Red Curry is full of Siamese flair while the Grilled Salmon Portuguese Sambal borrows from Malaccan Portuguese cuisine.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Gulai Lemak Udang Linguine (left). Grilled Salmon Portuguese Sambal (right). — Pictures courtesy of Kopimeo x La Carne
Sometimes the biggest transformation comes from switching things up ever slightly.
“In 2015, we came up with the Gulai Lemak Udang Linguine because I wanted to try using santan rather than cream in my pasta and somehow, it worked!” says Iena.
The dish also incorporates prawns and homemade lemongrass oil in place of olive oil, bringing together elements of local cooking and Italian pasta.

Then there is the aforementioned Spicy Salted Fish Pasta, inspired by her father’s habit of crumbling salted fish over pasta. At the restaurant, salted mackerel takes the place of anchovies, while daun kesum replaces parsley.
Desserts don’t fail to delight either: Expect crunchy cornflakes-crusted French toast, ice cream sandwiches and apam balik toasties.
For Iena, however, fusion is not simply a matter of combining ingredients from contrasting culinary traditions.

“My approach is to explore various cuisines and cooking techniques, then find ways to make certain flavours work for our local audience without losing the character of the original dish,” she explains.
Ultimately fusion food shouldn’t be fancy or finicky, but rather taste like home.
She adds, “It’s not about changing a dish just for the sake of fusion, but understanding how different ingredients and flavours can complement one another.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Desserts include crunchy cornflakes-crusted French toast and ice cream sandwiches. — Picture courtesy of Kopimeo x La Carne
Not all recipes worked, of course. A combination might sound promising on paper, but it must function as a complete dish before earning a place on the menu.
“We taste, tweak and taste again,” Iena says.
That same attention to consistency extends beyond the kitchen. Meor says the couple listens to customers, observing what they order repeatedly, what they return for and where improvements are needed.
Their aim is to maintain a balance between familiarity and discovery, giving regulars reasons to return while encouraging them to try something new.

“Customers may come in for a particular dish or something they’ve seen on social media, but what makes them return is often the overall experience: somewhere comfortable to meet friends or bring their families,” says Meor.
“Some customers who came to Kopimeo when they were younger now bring their own children. We don’t take that loyalty for granted.”

That sense of continuity is particularly meaningful for a business built around the idea of a neighbourhood gathering place. A meal, a conversation over coffee or simply a little time away from a busy day can become part of the experience customers remember.
The opening of their second branch in Elmina has brought another challenge: maintaining the identity of the original outlet while responding to a different neighbourhood.

Meor says expansion is not simply a matter of reproducing a successful formula. Each location has its own customer preferences, which influence everything from best-selling dishes to stock and purchasing decisions.

A central kitchen prepares the restaurant’s main sauces and marinades, helping standardise flavours across both outlets while making daily operations more manageable. Even so, the team continues to learn what works best in Elmina.

“Some dishes that are popular in Shah Alam don’t necessarily perform the same way in Elmina, and vice versa,” says Meor. “What works in one place won’t automatically work in another, so we let customers’ preferences guide our decisions.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Kopimeo x La Carne is built around the idea of a neighbourhood gathering place. — Pictures courtesy of Kopimeo x La Carne

Recognising each other’s strengths helps when they are working together as spouses. Meor tends to focus on operations and commercial considerations, while Iena brings her creative instincts to the food and menu.
“Work can follow you home when you’re in business together,” says Iena. “We don’t always need to agree, but we do need to respect each other’s perspectives.”
Looking back, Meor believes he would approach the business differently if given another chance.

“I’d probably start with just one or two really good menu items and focus on perfecting them before expanding,” he says. “Doing fewer things exceptionally well can be much more valuable than trying to do too many things at once.”

For the couple and, indeed, their customers, Kopimeo x La Carne is more than simply coffee or creative plates of pasta. It has become a space where everyone can feel at ease, share a meal of familiar flavours while discovering something fresh too.

84b0ee4d13c68e7b: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 7 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said the government is prepared to consider easing foreign worker approval requirements for sectors facing genuine manpower shortages, particularly the plantation sector.

Speaking at the 14th Forum Ilmuwan Malaysia Madani in Kuala Lumpur last night, Anwar said the proposal followed requests from industry players struggling to recruit workers for specific tasks, such as harvesting oil palm fruit.
He said approvals could be considered for such tasks, provided employers committed to reducing their reliance on foreign labour through mechanisation.
Anwar also said he had instructed the relevant authorities to simplify approval procedures for certain urgent labour needs.
“Plantations are asking for workers. I agree if they are specifically for harvesting, but many plantations also use them for other purposes.
“So, while I agree with the request, I think I will take this up with the relevant ministers.

“If the workers are specifically needed for harvesting, we can approve the request, provided they give an undertaking that they will reduce their dependence on foreign labour through mechanisation,” Anwar said.

He suggested reviewing how foreign workers are deployed within large plantations, including shifting manpower from adequately staffed activities to those facing shortages, which he described as a fairer arrangement.
Anwar also questioned why some plantations, despite substantial profits, had yet to invest meaningfully in automation and mechanisation to reduce their reliance on foreign labour.
He went on to criticise major companies for resisting wage increases despite substantial profits, citing one company that had made RM1 billion but was unwilling to raise monthly pay by just RM20.
Beyond labour shortages, Anwar raised concerns about the treatment of foreign workers, condemning exploitative practices by some employers.
“We bring in foreign workers, but sometimes the treatment is so dehumanising.
“We talk about Madani, social justice and so on, yet look at how some factories house their workers in conditions resembling those of slaves a hundred years ago.
“I cannot accept that,” he said.

Anwar also raised concerns over recruitment syndicates and excessive fees, saying the government was negotiating with individual source countries to reduce costs and protect workers from exploitation.
He stressed that recruitment fees must be reasonable and should not impose an undue financial burden on workers, particularly given the inflated charges imposed by some agents.
“Previously, agents would take workers’ wages and keep their passports. I describe this as modern slavery, and we cannot condone it.

“Although I agree, and I have taken important note of the concerns raised tonight about reviewing certain aspects of foreign worker requirements, including those for specific plantation activities, we must remember that there must be firm action against any form of abuse, including the exploitation of foreign workers.
“They are not our slaves, and excessive actions taken against foreigners are also unjustified,” he said.

The forum, which focused on national resilience in food security amid global uncertainties, was moderated by Anwar and attended by Agriculture and Food Security Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu, SD Guthrie Berhad Group President and CEO Mohd Haris Mohd Arshad, and PNB Research Institute CEO Sarena Che Omar.

5455525c43dd710d: NOVEMBER 7 — When Takashi Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus One roared into cinemas in late 2023, it didn’t just revitalise a legendary 70-year-old franchise, it fundamentally recalibrated what a kaiju movie could be.
It sat proudly right at the top of my favourite films list that year, a masterclass in balancing city flattening spectacle with tender, agonisingly human drama.
So, naturally, when news hit that Yamazaki was returning to helm the sequel, Godzilla Minus Zero, I found myself caught in that classic film geek dilemma.
On one hand, I was drooling with anticipation at the prospect of returning to this post-war Japan that was flattened not only by war, but also by a giant monster.

On the other hand, there was that very real, persistent dread that haunts every cinema lover, which is the curse of the inferior sequel. How could any follow-up possibly live up to the lightning-in-a-bottle perfection of its predecessor?

Well, I am overjoyed to report that I shouldn’t have worried at all. Godzilla Minus Zero isn’t just a worthy successor. It is every bit as thrilling, emotional, and utterly magnificent as Godzilla Minus One, and maybe even better!
Yamazaki has managed to preserve every single ingredient that made fans across the globe fall head over heels in love with the 2023 original.
The sense of pure, unadulterated awe is intact. The deeply relatable human roster remains the emotional anchor of the narrative.
Most importantly, that effortless, razor thin tightrope walk between being a roaring blockbuster monster movie and an intimate, character driven story is handled with supreme confidence once again.
It is simultaneously big and small, epic and personal, and in every measurable metric, all sorts of awesome. In short, this is what every blockbuster should be like, no matter where it may come from.
What truly elevates Godzilla Minus Zero, however, is how seamlessly it takes those core elements and amplifies them.

Backed by a noticeably bigger budget this time around (reportedly somewhere between US$15 million or RM60 million and US$50 million, compared to the US$10 million to US$15 million it took to make Godzilla Minus One), Yamazaki doesn’t waste a single cent of screen space.

The scale of the action set-pieces is grander, the visual effects work is even more pristine, and the destruction feels terrifyingly tangible. And don’t even get me started on the sound design, this film was shatteringly loud in the IMAX hall I was in!

Whether it’s the jaw-dropping introduction of King Ghidorah, whose chaotic, sky-rending presence will have genre fans squealing with pure delight and grinning like little kids again, or the sheer weight and menace of our favourite big bad Godzilla himself, the creature feature aspects deliver total cinematic euphoria.
Seeing these titan clashes mounted with such artistry on the big screen reminds you why we go to the movies in the first place.
Yet, as with Godzilla Minus One, the true secret weapon here isn’t the scale of the digital destruction, it’s the heart beating beneath the rubble.
The human narrative in Godzilla Minus Zero hits even harder than before, crafting an emotional arc that is genuinely wrenching.

Now, to be fair, some of the melodramatic beats and heightened emotional notes might feel a tad heavy handed or too melodramatic for Western audiences accustomed to the hyper-cynical tone of modern Hollywood blockbusters.

But for us Asian viewers, raised on narratives that aren’t afraid to wear their hearts shamelessly on their sleeves, it lands just perfect. You care deeply about these people, which makes every stomp of a giant foot feel like a high-stakes tragedy rather than empty spectacle.
Underneath all the kinetic chaos and tear-jerking character moments lies the film’s true crown jewel, its thematic weight.
What makes Godzilla Minus Zero stand so far above standard multiplex fare is the sharp, universal message it sends out to the world.
It pulls no punches in examining humanity’s insatiable, almost pathological lust for war and the relentless development of ever more destructive weaponry.

In a world that often feels perpetually on the brink of conflict, the film presents a profound counter-argument, which is that true strength lies not in superior firepower or endless retaliation, but in letting go of your thirst for vengeance.
It reminds us that choosing to embrace peace might just be the absolute best, and perhaps only, way for each one of us to move forward together.
It is rare for a creature feature to hit with such emotional clarity, let alone twice in a row.
Godzilla Minus Zero is a triumphant achievement in genre filmmaking that proves Godzilla Minus One was no fluke.
Bold, magnificent, and deeply moving, this is clearly one of the absolute best films of the year, and wow… it looks like Takashi Yamazaki is going to top my end-of-year list all over again.
* This is the personal opinion of the columnist.

5e05bdff2846cd38: There's something fascinating about the way politics can suddenly become everybody's conversation.
A development thousands of kilometres away, in a country with its own complicated political divisions, can find its way into Malaysian coffee-shop discussions, WhatsApp groups and social media feeds.
We may disagree about the personalities involved, but every so often, an election result makes us pause and pay attention.
The recent United States midterm elections offered one such moment.
Among the results attracting attention was Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan's Senate race, making him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
The Democrats also won control of both chambers of Congress, setting the stage for a significant shift in Washington.
Beyond the party numbers and political calculations, however, there's a more universal question worth considering: what do we actually want from our leaders?
It's easy to be drawn to the excitement of an election, the force of a campaign or the promise of a fresh face.
Representation matters, too.
Seeing people from different backgrounds enter positions of influence can challenge assumptions about who belongs in the room and whose voices deserve to be heard.
But a historic victory, impressive credentials or the ability to command attention do not, by themselves, make someone a good leader.

Leadership is ultimately tested in less glamorous moments: in the decisions made when nobody is watching, in the willingness to listen to people who disagree, and in the ability to accept responsibility when things go wrong, rather than searching for someone else to blame.
And perhaps most importantly, in what a person chooses to do with the power entrusted to them.
Such qualities develop over time, through experience, failure, mentorship and the everyday choices that reveal a person's character.
After all, most of us have encountered people who are exceptionally good at what they do but not necessarily good at bringing others along with them.
We've also met those who may not be the loudest voice in a room, yet have a way of earning trust, making people feel heard and helping a team find its footing when things become difficult.
The difference isn't always a matter of intelligence or ability.
Sometimes, it comes down to empathy, humility and an understanding that leadership isn't about having all the answers, but being willing to find them together.
Which brings the conversation closer to home.
Nurturing Future Leaders
In Malaysia, we often speak about developing future leaders as though it were a destination young people will eventually reach once they've accumulated enough qualifications and experience.
Yet leadership isn't something that suddenly appears with a job title.
It's something that needs to be nurtured long before a person occupies a position of authority.
Education is an important part of that journey, but perhaps we need to look beyond grades and qualifications when considering what makes someone worth investing in.

A young person may have the academic ability to excel, but do they also have the curiosity to understand the world around them, the humility to learn from others and the courage to stand by their convictions?
Can they recognise that the opportunities they receive also come with responsibilities?
Such qualities emerge in how a person responds to challenges, treats those with less influence and handles situations in which there's no easy or obvious answer.
This is why the experiences young people encounter outside the classroom matter, too.
Working with people from different backgrounds can challenge assumptions.
Volunteering can expose them to circumstances they might otherwise never encounter.
A good mentor can offer an uncomfortable but necessary perspective, helping a young person recognise not only their strengths, but also the blind spots they need to work on.
None of these experiences guarantees good leadership.
But they can help develop the judgement and self-awareness that positions of responsibility demand.
A scholarship, at its most meaningful, should do more than remove the financial barriers to education.
It should open minds, broaden experiences and help young people understand that success isn't solely a personal achievement.
Yayasan Khazanah (YK), which celebrates its 20th anniversary this year, is one example of this longer-term investment in Malaysian talent.

Beyond providing scholarship opportunities, its approach places emphasis on developing scholars as individuals through leadership and character development, mentorship, volunteering and exposure to different working environments.

The emphasis on personal and moral reasoning alongside academic ability reflects a wider understanding of potential: what matters is not only what a person knows, but how they use that knowledge and respond to responsibility.
There's a particularly meaningful idea behind this: that a scholarship isn't simply given to a person, but through that person.
In other words, the opportunity should eventually extend beyond the individual recipient, finding its way into the communities, workplaces and country that helped make it possible.
The impact of such an investment may not be immediately apparent.

It could emerge years later, when a scholar makes a difficult but principled decision at work, uses their expertise to address a problem affecting the wider community or takes the time to guide someone who's only beginning their own journey.
These aren't necessarily achievements that make headlines.
Yet they're among the ways knowledge and opportunity can travel further than the individual who first receives them.
Other Malaysian organisations, including Yayasan Sime Darby and PETRONAS, also invest in developing young talent through education sponsorships and broader development opportunities.
Their programmes may differ, but the underlying recognition is similar: the country needs more than academically accomplished graduates.
It needs people who can apply their knowledge with sound judgement, integrity and a sense of purpose.
There's also a question of access. Talent exists in every community, but opportunities to develop it aren't always equally available.
Financial support can remove one barrier, while mentoring and exposure to different environments can help young people recognise possibilities they may not previously have imagined.
Investing in future leaders, then, isn't simply about finding those who already appear exceptional.
It's also about giving capable young people the support and room to grow, while helping them understand that opportunity carries an obligation to use it well.
The Character of a Society
Of course, no scholarship programme can guarantee that its recipients will become exemplary leaders.
Character cannot be handed out with an award letter, just as integrity cannot be taught in a single training session.
Both must be practised and tested in the decisions people make when no one is telling them what to do.
That's why the example set by the people around young leaders matters so much.
Young people learn not only from what they're told, but from what they observe.

They notice whether people in positions of authority admit mistakes, whether differing opinions are welcomed and whether the values spoken about so confidently are actually reflected in everyday decisions.
A culture that rewards achievement without questioning how it's attained risks producing people who know how to succeed but have given less thought to what their success should serve.
But giving young people access to education, broadening their experiences and surrounding them with people who can guide and challenge them creates the conditions in which leadership can grow.
That's an investment whose returns may take years to become visible.

Perhaps that's the true measure of investing in future generations: not the qualifications earned, careers established or doors opened, but what people eventually do with the opportunities they've received.
The next generation of leaders will not all enter politics.
Some will become doctors, teachers, entrepreneurs, civil servants, scientists or community organisers.
Others may never hold particularly grand titles, yet will shape lives through the way they work, treat colleagues, raise families or stand up for someone whose voice might otherwise go unheard.
Their contributions may never make headlines or earn public recognition.
Yet leadership isn't measured by titles or visibility alone.
It's also found in the quiet choices that make a difference to others, the opportunities created for those who follow and the values passed on along the way.
These are the people who shape the character of a society.
Perhaps that's the more lasting lesson behind our fascination with elections and political milestones.
We spend considerable time debating who deserves to lead us, but far less considering how we prepare people to lead well.
A ballot can confer authority, a qualification can open doors and an institution can provide opportunity.
But none of these, on their own, can make someone a good leader.
That depends on the values they carry and what they choose to do with the opportunities entrusted to them.
If we want a future shaped by leaders who are capable, compassionate and conscious of their responsibilities, the work must begin long before they step into the spotlight.

1054885c3338c26d: MELAKA: When Vong Fook Hoi first approached Noor Helmy Abdul Halem for help, the elderly Chinese man had little reason to trust a Barisan Nasional (BN) politician.
It was 2020, and although BN had unexpectedly returned as part of the state government in Melaka, most people, including Vong, were still unhappy with the coalition.
A simple appeal for welfare assistance ultimately brought the two men together, blossoming into a friendship that has become a regular feature of Helmy's public engagements and social media videos.
Helmy, then a councillor with the Malacca Historic City Council, said Vong was 82 when he came for help, having applied for old-age assistance since he was 60 without success.
“He kept that anger for 20 years. Maybe he applied once and didn’t get it. After that, he was disappointed and never tried again, that is, until he came to me," he told FMT.

Helmy said all he did was help submit Vong’s application, but the successful outcome marked the beginning of a friendship that continued even after he was elected Duyong assemblyman in the 2021 state election.
Over time, Vong began to trust him and bring other residents’ complaints to his attention.
The Umno man credited Vong, now 88, with helping him understand the concerns of Chinese residents, including what made them unhappy and why they felt disconnected from the government.
"The harmony we see today did not happen overnight. The trust deficit was very big prior to this," he said.
"There were issues of trust, misunderstandings and major communication breakdowns. I tried to address these issues and resolve them one by one."
For Vong, that trust was built through Helmy’s willingness to help, even in matters outside the usual demands of an elected representative.
He recounted calling Helmy at about 1.30am one night when he was unwell and needed to see a doctor.
“He was sleeping, but he woke up and came to pick me up,” Vong said.
On another occasion, Helmy bought Vong a new bicycle after noticing the condition of his old one, despite Vong insisting that there was nothing wrong with it.
Such gestures have helped turn Vong into one of Helmy’s most recognisable supporters.
Known as “Uncle Wong”, he frequently appears in the assemblyman’s social media videos. Vong rejects the suggestion that his support has been motivated by money.
“Please do not misunderstand me. I am not saying all this because he gives me money. It is not about that. He genuinely cares for the people,” Vong said.
He said Helmy treats everyone with the same respect, regardless of race.
“He treats Chinese, Malays, Indians and everyone else well. He does not say he only wants to look after his own people,” Vong added.
Helmy said he has never paid Vong anything, and that Vong joined campaigns “out of his trust in me”.
He said his social media videos were also a way to explain local services and correct misconceptions about government assistance.

For example, Helmy said residents had frequently complained about grass-cutting services before videos were made explaining the schedule and standards, including that grass should not exceed 5cm after cutting.
He said the number of complaints has since fallen, with those that remain being specific in nature.
Helmy said he hopes to win another term to complete “unfinished work”, including projects first initiated by his predecessor, Damian Yeo of DAP.

"One of these is a health clinic in Duyong. It was first initiated by Damian. He was the one who proposed the site behind the Japerun. I continued what had been started, and today it is close to being implemented," he said.
As for Vong, he said he would be sad if Helmy lost the election on Nov 14.
"I really, really hope he wins this year. He cannot lose. I hope he wins. I even pray to Tian Gong (the Jade Emperor) to help him win because he is just too good a person," he said.
Helmy is facing Pakatan Harapan’s Poo Long Suan in a straight fight for the Duyong seat.
25e09d5b8c6e18e4: GEORGE TOWN: In the Indian state of Keralam - previously Kerala - wellness is not tucked away behind the doors of a clinic. It is increasingly woven into the travel experience itself, alongside its backwaters, beaches, lush landscapes and cultural attractions.

Keralam has built a strong reputation around Ayurveda, the traditional system of healing that uses herbs, oils, diet, massage and other therapies to support well-being. For many visitors, that means a holiday can include anything from a short treatment to a longer stay centred on a personalised wellness programme.

Bernama saw that model first-hand during a recent trip there to cover Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s official visit, including a stop at The Raviz Kadavu resort in Calicut. There, an Ayurvedic centre operates within the hotel grounds, allowing guests to combine treatment with the comfort and slower pace of a resort stay.

Ayurvedic physician Dr Roufi Ahammed C said one of the biggest misconceptions is that Ayurveda is simply another word for massage. In reality, he said, it takes a much broader view of health and lifestyle.
“Ayurveda is a way of living,” he said. “It is linked with food, medicine, massage, treatment, external therapy, yoga and meditation.”

At the resort, guests can stay in a conventional hotel setting while undergoing Ayurvedic treatment, receiving herbal medicines and eating meals prepared according to their programme. Some travel to Keralam specifically for Ayurveda, while others simply add a treatment or two to a wider holiday.

The state has also introduced a classification system for Ayurveda centres, with Ayur Silver, Ayur Gold and Ayur Diamond ratings based on factors such as cleanliness, staff qualifications, safety standards, patient records and the quality of treatment facilities.
For travellers, that provides a useful measure of reassurance in a sector where standards and approaches can vary considerably.

Roufi stressed, however, that Ayurveda should not be approached casually simply because many of its medicines are plant-based. Herbal treatments can still have side effects, while conventional medicine remains essential in emergencies and for conditions requiring immediate medical intervention.
“Both systems, Ayurveda and modern medicine, have their own roles and limitations,” he said, pointing out that someone suffering a heart attack, for example, needs urgent conventional medical care.
The value of Ayurveda, he suggested, lies not in replacing modern medicine wholesale but in understanding where each approach may have a role.

Another fundamental principle is personalisation: Roufi said two people with the same complaint may receive different medicines, therapies and dietary advice because treatment takes into account each person’s constitution and overall condition.
"You and your friend can come for the same condition, but the medicines and treatment provided can be different because both of you are different individuals," he stressed.

Longer programmes can also demand considerable time and preparation. Panchakarma, one of the better-known Ayurvedic programmes, traditionally involves a series of cleansing procedures and cannot simply be started immediately upon arrival.
Roufi compared the process to waiting for fruit to ripen. At his centre, he said, the full programme requires at least 21 days, allowing the body to be prepared before the main procedures begin.
“We cannot directly take juice from a raw mango. We have to ripen it,” he said. “Similar to that, we have to prepare our body for panchakarma.”
Could Malaysia learn from Keralam?

K Saravana Kumar, Malaysia’s consul-general in South India, believes Keralam’s experience could offer useful lessons for Malaysia as interest in wellness tourism grows. He pointed to the state’s long experience in traditional medicine, along with research and efforts to integrate Ayurveda with conventional healthcare.

“There is a lot of research being carried out that can be explored by Malaysian experts or entrepreneurs in collaboration with healthcare practitioners and established Ayurvedic institutions in Keralam," he suggested.
For Malaysia, he noted, the opportunity would be to develop wellness offerings carefully, with clear standards and appropriate regulation rather than simply copying India's model.

Keralam’s appeal lies partly in how seamlessly Ayurveda sits within the wider travel experience, alongside its food, landscapes and cultural traditions. Perhaps that is the real lesson for Malaysia: wellness tourism works best when it feels not like an add-on, but an essential part of the journey.
1e9843a9fbc4a8ec: MELAKA: Vong Fook Hoi tidak menaruh sepenuh kepercayaan terhadap ahli politik Barisan Nasional (BN) ketika pertama kali meminta bantuan daripada Noor Helmy Abdul Halem pada 2020.
Walaupun tanpa dijangka BN kembali menjadi sebahagian daripada kerajaan Melaka, kebanyakan orang termasuk Vong masih tidak berpuas hati dengan gabungan itu.
Permintaan ringkas untuk mendapatkan bantuan kebajikan berkembang menjadi persahabatan dan kini sebahagian daripada aktiviti awam Helmy serta video di media sosialnya.

Helmy yang ketika itu ahli Majlis Bandaraya Melaka Bersejarah (MBMB) berkata, Vong berusia 82 tahun ketika tampil meminta bantuannya, selepas gagal dalam permohonan bantuan warga emas sejak berusia 60 tahun.

"Dia menyimpan kemarahan itu selama 20 tahun. Mungkin dia pernah mohon sekali, tetapi gagal. Selepas itu, dia kecewa dan tidak pernah cuba lagi sehinggalah dia datang berjumpa saya," katanya kepada FMT.

Helmy berkata, beliau hanya membantu mengemukakan permohonan Vong, tetapi kejayaan permohonan itu menjadi titik permulaan kepada persahabatan mereka, walaupun selepas beliau dipilih sebagai Adun Duyong pada PRN Melaka 2021.
Lama-kelamaan, Vong mula menaruh kepercayaan terhadap Helmy dan membawa aduan penduduk lain kepadanya.
Ahli politik Umno itu menyifatkan Vong, yang kini 88 tahun, banyak membantunya memahami keresahan masyarakat Cina, termasuk rasa tidak puas hati dan sebab mereka berasa terpinggir daripada kerajaan.
"Keharmonian yang kita lihat hari ini tidak terbina dalam sekelip mata. Sebelum ini, jurang kepercayaan antara masyarakat dan kerajaan sangat besar.
"Terdapat isu kepercayaan, salah faham dan kegagalan komunikasi yang ketara. Saya cuba menangani semua isu ini dan menyelesaikannya satu demi satu."
Bagi Vong pula, kepercayaan itu terbina daripada kesediaan Helmy menghulurkan bantuan, termasuk dalam perkara yang melangkaui tanggungjawab biasa wakil rakyat.
Antaranya, beliau pernah menghubungi Helmy kira-kira 1.30 pagi ketika kurang sihat dan memerlukan rawatan doktor.
"Dia sedang tidur, tetapi dia bangun dan datang menjemput saya," kata Vong.
Helmy pernah membeli sebuah basikal baharu untuk Vong selepas melihat keadaan basikal lamanya, walaupun warga emas itu berkeras basikalnya masih boleh digunakan.
Keprihatinan sedemikian menjadikan Vong antara penyokong Helmy yang paling dikenali.
Dikenali sebagai Uncle Wong, beliau kerap muncul dalam video Adun itu di media sosial. Vong menolak tanggapan sokongannya terhadap Helmy didorong wang.

"Tolong jangan salah faham. Saya bukan katakan semua ini kerana dia beri saya wang. Bukan itu sebabnya. Dia benar-benar prihatin terhadap rakyat," kata Vong sambil menambah Helmy melayan semua orang tanpa mengira kaum dengan penuh hormat.
"Dia melayan masyarakat Cina, Melayu, India dan semua orang dengan baik. Dia tidak pernah kata hanya mahu menjaga kaumnya sendiri."
Helmy pula berkata, beliau tidak pernah memberikan wang kepada Vong, yang menyertai kempennya "kerana percaya terhadap saya".
Jelasnya, video media sosialnya bertujuan menerangkan perkhidmatan setempat dan membetulkan salah tanggapan terhadap bantuan kerajaan.

Sebagai contoh, katanya, penduduk sering mengadu perkhidmatan pemotongan rumput sebelum video dihasilkan bagi menjelaskan jadual dan piawaian ditetapkan, termasuk rumput tidak boleh melebihi 5cm selepas dipotong.
Beliau berkata, jumlah aduan berkurangan sejak itu dan aduan masih ada lebih bersifat khusus.
Helmy berharap dapat mempertahankan kerusi Duyong selama satu penggal lagi untuk menyelesaikan "tugas belum selesai", termasuk projek yang mula dirancang bekas penyandang daripada DAP, Damian Yeo.

"Antaranya, pembinaan sebuah klinik kesihatan di Duyong. Ia dimulakan Damian. Beliau yang mencadangkan tapak di belakang Japerun di sini. Saya teruskan apa yang telah dimulakan dan kini ia hampir ke peringkat pelaksanaan."

Bagi Vong: "Saya benar-benar harap dia menang tahun ini. Dia tidak boleh kalah. Saya harap dia menang. Saya turut berdoa kepada Tian Gong (Maharaja Jed) untuk membantunya menang kerana dia terlalu baik."
Helmy akan berentap dengan calon Pakatan Harapan (PH), Poo Long Suan dalam pertembungan satu lawan satu bagi merebut DUN Duyong.
84ff9971a848ea4b: RUSSIAN qualifier Alexandra Shubladze shocked top seed Sorana Cirstea 6-2, 6-3 on Friday at the Prudential Hong Tennis Open to advance to her first tour- level semifinal.

Shubladze, 21, registered her first win over a top-20 player against Romania's Cirstea, a 36-year-old ranked 15th. Shubladze, who is making her tour-level debut and is ranked No. 136, had not previously faced a top-30 opponent.
She won 5 of 8 break-point opportunities and saved 7 of 8 in the match lasting one hour, 27 minutes. She will face American Claire Lui, who defeated Zeynep Sonmez of Turkey 6-1, 6-4.

Second-seeded Alexandra Eala of the Philippines won a battle with Croatia's Antonia Ruzic 7-6 (7), 7-5 to advance to the semifinals against fourth-seeded Maria Sakkari of Greece, who eliminated Aliaksandra Sasnovich of Belarus 6-2, 6-3.
Top seed Janice Tjen rallied past sixth-seeded Polina Kudermetova of Uzbekistan 5-7, 6-4, 6-2 in the quarterfinals of the WTA 250 event in India.
Tjen, of Indonesia, continues her title defense after powering to victory behind 13 aces to just two double faults. She faced four break points, saving two, while Kudermetova saved 8 of 12.

Third-seeded Magda Linette of Poland also had a winning response to dropping the first set in a 4-6, 7-5, 6-4 victory over Japan's Mai Hontama. Linette faces seventh-seeded Anastasia Zakharova in the semifinals.

Zakharova of Russia dispatched 10th-seeded Lucrezia Stefanini, with the Italian retiring with a lower-leg injury down 6-2, 5-2 in the quarterfinal match. American Robin Montgomery ousted another unseeded player, Maaya Rajeshwaran Revathi of India 6-3, 6-3, to earn a semifinal match against Tjen. — REUTERS
7c09dba9a66dc538: KUALA LUMPUR: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says he is prepared to consider approving the recruitment of foreign workers for palm oil harvesting, provided plantation companies commit to reducing their reliance on labour through mechanisation.
Speaking at a forum here yesterday, Anwar acknowledged the industry's labour needs but stressed that companies must invest in mechanisation.
He was responding to a question from an industry representative, who said delays in approving foreign worker quotas could affect palm oil production next year.
The representative said that machinery was already used for fertilising and weed control, but harvesting still depended heavily on manual labour.
Anwar said he would raise the matter with the relevant ministry and examine the request.
“If it is specifically for harvesting, okay. We will approve that. But you must then give an undertaking to reduce your reliance on foreign workers through mechanisation,” he said.

Anwar also criticised profitable plantation companies for failing to invest sufficiently in mechanisation and stressed that the exploitation of foreign workers, including placing them in poor living conditions, was unacceptable.

On broader agricultural reforms, the prime minister called for smallholders to be included in modernisation efforts, warning that excessive reliance on subsidies and assistance could perpetuate dependency.
Meanwhile, agriculture and food security minister Mohamad Sabu said the agricultural sector's contribution to the economy had grown significantly over the past two years.
“The agricultural sector's contribution to the country's GDP has increased by more than RM5 billion over the past two years,” he said.

Mohamad said more university graduates, including those with engineering backgrounds, were venturing into modern agriculture, with some becoming millionaires through aquaculture and high-value crop cultivation.
acf0028605cfead9: KUALA LUMPUR: Pas has demanded an explanation from the government over the delay in implementing former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak's house arrest despite the payment of his RM50 million fine.
Its secretary-general Datuk Seri Takiyuddin Hassan questioned why the Attorney-General's Chambers (A-GC) was still seeking clarification on the conditional royal pardon granted nearly two months ago.

He said the pardon, announced by the Legal Affairs Division of the Prime Minister's Department on Sept 18, clearly stipulated that Najib could serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of the fine.

"Under the ordinary interpretation of the law, and as understood by the public, it is clear that once the RM50 million fine has been paid, Najib should be allowed to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028," Takiyuddin said in a statement today.
He said the A-GC's claim that two possible interpretations of the royal pardon and the High Court's order required further examination should no longer arise.

He also questioned why the A-GC had not sought clarification earlier if its concerns were related to the High Court's rejection of an application for a stay of execution in Najib's separate 1Malaysia Development Bhd (1MDB) case on Oct 14.

"If that is the issue requiring examination and consideration, the A-GC should have sought clarification from the court on that date, rather than after Najib's supporters had gone to great lengths to raise funds to settle the fine imposed on him," he said.
Takiyuddin called on the A-GC to explain why the implementation of the royal pardon appeared to have been delayed.

"The government, particularly the A-GC as the guardian of the public interest, must provide a clear explanation to the public, without hiding behind excuses, as to why the implementation of the sentence appears to have been delayed," he said.
He said the legal maxim "justice delayed is justice denied" must be upheld to ensure fairness to all parties.
Yesterday, Umno confirmed that Najib's RM50 million fine had been paid in full at the Kuala Lumpur High Court.

However, the A-GC subsequently called for the implementation of his house arrest to be temporarily deferred pending clarification of legal questions surrounding the conditional pardon and the effect of the court orders.

The A-GC said the clarification was necessary to determine whether payment of the fine settled only the financial penalty, leaving Najib to serve the remainder of his SRC International prison sentence under house arrest, or whether it meant the entire sentence had been completed.
The chambers maintained that the proposed deferment was not intended to challenge the King's decree but to ensure that the pardon and related court orders were implemented correctly.
Najib's lawyers have rejected the A-GC's position and demanded his immediate transfer to house arrest.
Najib remains at Kajang Prison, where he has been serving his sentence since August 2022 following his conviction for misappropriating RM42 million in SRC International funds.
His original 12-year prison sentence and RM210 million fine were reduced to six years and RM50 million respectively by the Pardons Board in 2024.
72a4d55ba96bb0e6: WASHINGTON: Production of Cybertrucks -- the pickups hailed by enthusiasts as a symbol of Elon Musk's futuristic ambitions and equally hated as ugly reminders of the Donald Trump era -- will wind down, the Tesla CEO said Friday.
Tesla will stop building the truck at its Texas factory around the middle of 2027 to free up space for its Cybercab robotaxi, Musk said.
"Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk wrote on X.
Musk did not say whether the truck would be built elsewhere or discontinued altogether, nor what would happen to outstanding orders.
Wes Morrill, the Cybertruck's lead engineer, wrote in a separate post that the truck "was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."
"Thanks to everyone who contributed to making the future (look) like the future," he added.
Tesla fans lamented the departure of the Cybertruck on X, the social media platform Musk owns, but the tycoon reassured them that the Cybertruck fleet "will be around for a long time".

The truck came to be seen as an extension of Musk himself, and its image became entangled with his politics as he took on a high-profile role leading the Trump administration's cost-cutting department of government efficiency. Some owners reported vandalism and harassment.
The angular stainless-steel behemoth was unveiled in November 2019, and Musk said at the time it had drawn 250,000 preorders within days.
Production was originally slated for 2021 but was repeatedly delayed, with customer deliveries starting in late 2023.
Tesla built its Texas lines with planned capacity of 250,000 trucks a year, but sales have come nowhere near that figure.
As US demand slumped, Tesla began selling the truck abroad, starting deliveries in South Korea in November 2025 and in the UAE in January.
Tesla does not break out Cybertruck revenue, but its "other models" category, which includes the pickup, accounts for just a small percentage of sales.
Cox Automotive estimated total sales of just 72,702, with more than half in 2024 and fading thereafter.
The truck has also been subject to multiple recalls and complaints over build quality.
The Cybercab, a two-seat vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals, was unveiled in October 2024.
Tesla began production at the Texas plant in April and started offering paid Cybercab rides in Austin in September through its existing Robotaxi service.

"The decision to discontinue the Cybertruck highlights how difficult it can be to translate strong initial attention and enthusiasm around a new vehicle into sustainable mainstream demand," said Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive.
Tesla saw the vehicle as a bid for the giant US pickup truck market, but it quickly became a "niche" product, Valdez Streaty said.

The robotaxi is central to Musk's effort to recast Tesla as an artificial intelligence and robotics company rather than a carmaker, though its success depends on the company delivering fully driverless technology, which it has yet to demonstrate at scale.

c294bb45376b6b9a: LONDON: Prince Harry on Friday launched a legal challenge after losing a privacy case against the publisher of the British tabloid the Daily Mail.
The case is the third and final one brought by the Duke of Sussex in his acrimonious legal battle with British tabloids.

The High Court in August ordered Harry and six others, including pop legend Elton John, to make an initial payment of £9.5 million (US$13 million) to Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL) after finding against them a month earlier.

Harry, the 42-year-old younger son of King Charles III, and the other claimants were seeking to appeal on the grounds that the judgment and costs ruling were "legally and factually flawed", a statement sent to AFP by law firm Sheridans said.
The group had "today filed applications with the Court of Appeal for permission to appeal", the statement added.

The claimants in the case — who also include John's husband David Furnish and actors Elizabeth Hurley and Sadie Frost — had accused the Mail of bugging their cars and homes, listening in on calls and other privacy breaches. ANL had denied all the allegations.
The appeal bid comes after Harry, formally known as the Duke of Sussex, and his wife Meghan, 45, moved back to the UK in August with their two young children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five.
The couple left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a bitter royal family feud.

After an emotional 11-week trial — during which Harry gave in-person evidence — judge Matthew Nicklin in July sided with the newspaper publisher, concluding that the claimants had failed to prove their allegations.
After a further two-day hearing over costs, he made the initial costs decision, while again criticising the claimants' case as "speculative".
The court noted that ANL estimated its total costs defending itself had reached about £34.5 million by July 9.
However, the ruling noted that the High Court had not determined how much of those costs the claimants must ultimately pay.
The matter is set to be determined at a separate hearing.
Nicklin rejected requests by Harry and the others to pay
8690f9d6aef6da96: KUALA LUMPUR: Grain by grain, Sivabalan Arumugam transforms ordinary rice grains into intricate works of art.
With nimble hands, he moves across the floor, bringing vibrant kolam designs to life.
For the 36-year-old founder of Life Creation and Design Rangoli Kolam, the temporary nature of his creations has never dampened his passion for the traditional art form.
His fascination with colour has fuelled a lifelong commitment to preserving the craft while finding new ways to bring it into modern spaces.
Sivabalan has spent nearly 21 years working professionally in the field, having started at the age of 15. His creations have adorned shopping malls and office spaces.
His dedication earned him a place in the Malaysia Book of Records in October 2024 for creating the "Most Colours in a Single Rangoli Kolam".
The record-setting creation measured 20 x 25 feet and featured 100 distinct shades, with Sivabalan coming up with the entire design himself.
His interest in kolam began at the age of 7, when he started creating designs at home during festive occasions such as Deepavali and Pongal.
"My father could draw very well as a mechanical engineer, and I learnt from him. I really love colours. Whenever I draw a kolam, I feel happy," he said.
Trained in graphic design, Sivabalan handles both the design and execution of his creations, relying largely on freehand techniques rather than ready-made patterns.
He draws inspiration from books, online videos and textiles, as well as frequent trips to India, where he observes locals creating kolam outside their homes and in temples.
"Every day, the people, including women and children, design kolam in front of their houses and temples.
"The kolam they draw uses only white kolam powder, which is different from the kolam we make in Malaysia," he said.
His eye for colour combinations has led him to experiment with different shades, giving each design its own character.
But bringing each design to life requires months of painstaking preparation.
Rather than relying entirely on commercially available coloured rice, Sivabalan prepares his own using broken rice and food colouring, including jelly and cake colouring.
ART THAT DOESN'T LAST
For all the hours spent preparing and arranging the rice grains, a kolam remains a temporary creation.
A large installation can take three to four months to prepare and several days to complete, only to be cleared soon after the celebrations end.
"It is sad seeing the kolam swept away after hours of hard work. But that's just how the process goes when making a kolam.
"We can only look forward to next year's celebration and come up with newer designs to make our kolam even better," Sivabalan said.
PASSING IT ON TO THE NEXT GENERATION
For Sivabalan, the fleeting nature of kolam is a reminder to value not just the finished creation, but also the skill, patience and preparation behind it.
He believes the tradition can survive only if it is passed on to those willing to learn and practise the craft, particularly younger generations.
"I definitely want to teach the younger generation so they can appreciate the culture and it won't be forgotten," he said.

f4409c2630f1bd35: From Moaz Nair

We must all extend our heartfelt gratitude to PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang. For decades, ordinary Malaysians have blundered through political disagreements using tedious, secular terms like "policy differences", "economic discrepancies" or "constitutional debates". How utterly pedestrian.

As a vanguard of religious leadership, the PAS supremo has single-handedly elevated local political discourse into an apocalyptic battleground. While political analysts and opposition figures may fret over his "highly polarising language", they simply lack the vision to appreciate the sheer artistry of his negative vocabulary. For those trying to understand how a man so deeply versed in Islam chooses to navigate the political arena, here is a handy guide to his masterclass in decorum.
'Dajjal' doctrine

Why debate the terms of a standard legislative agreement when you can invoke the literal embodiment of evil? In November, when the government and opposition floated a routine confidence and supply agreement, ordinary leaders might have debated fiscal allocations. Not the maestro. Hadi swiftly diagnosed the cross-party truce as a "Dajjal approach at the end of times". By equating a political compromise to the false Messiah, he reminded us all that bipartisanship isn't just bad governance – it is practically the precursor to Armageddon.
Advanced sociology

In 2022, Hadi gracefully simplified the complex, systemic issue of financial crime. While anti-corruption agencies waste millions studying institutional loopholes, Hadi cracked the code by declaring non-Muslims and non-Bumiputeras the "roots of corruption" in Malaysia. When civil society groups like Transparency International Malaysia cried foul over xenophobia, they clearly missed the theological nuance: why fix a broken system when you can just blame a demographic?
Grammar lessons

Parliamentary decorum is so last century. In 2025, during a serious parliamentary debate, Hadi decided to give the Dewan Rakyat a live lesson in the finer points of the national language. When referring to a small group of white Westerners, he bypassed standard human pronouns entirely and opted for the animal classifier "ekor" (tails). While lawmakers questioned his basic courtesy, language purists had to admire his commitment to treating geopolitical adversaries like stray livestock.
Intellectual plebeians

Consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds. When four Malay DAP leaders had the audacity to question Hadi's shifting ideological stances over the years, he didn’t bother wasting precious scripture on them. Instead, he publicly dismissed them as "kurang berpendidikan" (uneducated). It is a flawless debate tactic: if someone points out an inconsistency, simply remind them they lack the spiritual PhD required to comprehend it.
Friendship flexibility

Over the decades, the PAS supremo has treated political alliances like fashion seasons – highly disposable and entirely dependent on the weather. Consider his decades-long dance with DAP. During the golden years of the Barisan Alternatif and Pakatan Rakyat coalitions (1999–2013), Hadi shared the stage with the very same DAP leaders he now rebukes. Back then, political cooperation (tahaluf siyasi) was championed as a noble, strategic pursuit.

Fast forward to the 2015 PAS muktamar, where the party abruptly severed ties with DAP without debate. Overnight, the former allies were retroactively transformed into the ultimate ideological adversaries. Progressive PAS members who dared to question this sudden U-turn were thoroughly purged, eventually leaving to form the splinter party Amanah.

The flexibility didn't stop there. By 2019, Hadi had signed the Muafakat Nasional pact with Umno – the absolute arch-nemesis his infamous 1981 "Amanat Hadi" had once forcefully condemned. By 2020, he pivoted again to anchor Perikatan Nasional. It is a masterclass in situational theology: an alliance is perfectly holy right up until the exact moment it becomes politically inconvenient, at which point it is scrubbed from historical memory.
Political safari

When he is not channelling the end-times, our grand maestro moonlights as a visionary political safari guide, earning the fond moniker of an "amateur zoologist". Under his taxonomic eye, a battered Umno was famously diagnosed as a hobbled "itik patah kaki" (lame duck) to justify PAS seizing the steering wheel.

Meanwhile, secular opportunists and those demanding Western-style updates are swiftly demoted to "binatang yang tidak berakal" (senseless animals). Should you dare criticise his shifting paradigms, you are seamlessly categorised into his menagerie as either a hyperactive "kera" (monkey), a relentlessly barking "anjing" (dog) or a "babi" (pig). Naturally, this rich pedagogical blueprint has inspired his disciples – PAS lawmakers recently took flight into the aviary, branding Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim a "burung tiong" (myna bird) to mock him as a mindless echo chamber for external policies.
Linguistic irony

This leads us to the ultimate comedic paradox of modern Malaysian politics: the profound irony of utilising the sacred vocabulary of the heavens to conduct everyday, transactional mud-slinging. Islam possesses a rich linguistic tradition designed to inspire spiritual contemplation and universal grace. Yet, in the hands of the PAS leadership, this vocabulary is weaponised as a highly specialised political toolkit.

When routine legislative agreements are framed through the lens of Islamic eschatology, a standard, secular agreement is artificially inflated into a cosmic battle between divine light and ultimate darkness. By deploying heavy theological concepts to score cheap points in the daily 24-hour news cycle, the sacred is systematically cheapened.

The greatest irony lies in the moral inversion it creates. While the faith heavily emphasises humility, restraint and the avoidance of slander, this brand of political rhetoric uses the language of the faith to justify the exact opposite: alienating minor demographics, dismissing critics as intellectually inferior and reducing foreign visitors to animal classifiers.
Entertaining spectacle

While monitoring bodies like the Centre for Independent Journalism track his vocabulary as a major driver of identity-based division, defenders stand firm, arguing this uncompromising tone is a steadfast defence of faith.

And who can blame them? Nothing screams "peaceful, universal faith" quite like reducing your neighbours to corrupt roots, your parliamentary colleagues to animals and basic governance to the work of the false Messiah.

Ultimately, this strategy yields a highly entertaining spectacle. By insisting that every standard political manoeuvre is either an act of divine necessity or a plot by the Dajjal, the political arena becomes an absurdist theatre – proving that nothing elevates a secular turf war quite like a heavy dusting of fire and brimstone.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.
